Before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of dark water, and above it slept a silver bird named Avaru. In her dream she heard a child crying beneath the waves. She opened one eye, and that eye became the moon.

Avaru dove into the black sea and found no child, only a glowing seed. She carried it in her beak, but it burned with loneliness, so she cracked it upon the water. From the shell rose the first island, warm and green. From the yolk sprang the sun, leaping into the sky. From the white came clouds, sheep-soft and wandering.

Still the seed’s heart beat sadly. Avaru plucked seven feathers from her breast and planted them in the island’s soil. At sunset, they became people. They were small and frightened, so Avaru taught them to laugh by shaking rain from her wings. She taught them to sing by calling to the tides.

When Avaru grew old, she flew upward and scattered herself across the night. Her feathers became stars. That is why, when people are lost, they look above: the mother bird is still guiding her children home with bright, unblinking eyes.

Long ago, before rivers knew their paths, the world was a silent bowl of dust. In its center slept Aro, the Stone Giant, curled beneath a blanket of hills. Above him wandered Luma, a small blue star who had fallen from the night and could not climb home.

Each evening, Luma sang to the sky, but the heavens were too far to answer. Her tears dropped onto the dust, making silver pools. The pools joined, becoming streams that tickled Aro’s ears. At last he woke, stretched his enormous arms, and cracked the earth open.

“Why do you weep, little flame?” he asked.

“I am lost,” said Luma. “I belong among my sisters.”

Aro felt pity. He gathered the tallest mountains and stacked them one upon another. Luma climbed, but still the sky was beyond her reach. So Aro broke a piece from his own shining heart and lifted it high. It became the moon, a bridge of pale fire.

Luma stepped onto it and returned to heaven. In gratitude, she guided the streams Aro had awakened, teaching them to run toward the sea.

That is why rivers shine at night: they remember the fallen star who gave them their first song.

Myth: In the first age, the world lay hushed beneath a roof of endless dark. No river moved, no bird called, and the mountains were only dreams sleeping under dust. Beneath the highest hill rested Orun, the Giant of Stone, whose heart glowed softly like an ember. Above him drifted Seli, a wandering star-child who had slipped from the sky and fallen to earth.

Seli tried each night to sing herself home, but her voice broke into tears. Where the tears touched the ground, clear pools opened; where the pools overflowed, streams began to crawl like silver snakes. Their cold fingers woke Orun, who rose with a groan that shaped the valleys.

“Why do you flood my sleep?” he asked.

“I have lost the road to my people,” Seli whispered.

Orun lifted mountains upon his shoulders, but the sky remained too far. So he opened his chest and gave Seli half his burning heart. She set it above the world, and it became the moon, a shining stair through darkness.

Seli climbed back to the heavens. Yet before she vanished, she blessed the new waters with memory. That is why rivers gleam under moonlight: they are carrying a star’s farewell toward the sea.

Myth: Before the first dawn, the world was a hollow shell drifting on a black sea. Inside it slept Erua, the white-winged heron, with her head tucked beneath one wing. In her sleep she heard a song rising from below, a lonely note so small it made the darkness tremble.

Erua opened her beak and called back. Her call became the wind. She dipped her long legs into the sea and stirred until the waters curled into circles. From the deepest circle floated a blue stone, warm as a heartbeat. Erua carried it upward and set it upon the waves.

The stone softened into the first land. Moss grew where her feet had touched it, and trees rose where drops fell from her feathers. Yet the lonely song continued. Erua pressed her breast to the earth, and seven sparks fluttered out. They became the first people, blinking beneath the new sun.

They did not know where to walk, so Erua drew rivers with her beak to guide them. They did not know how to hope, so she scattered bright seeds into the sky.

Those seeds became stars, and every night they sing the small song back to the sea.

Myth: Before dawn learned its name, the world was a dark egg afloat on endless water. Within it dreamed Ivara, the gray crane, listening to a thin music rising from the deep. She tapped the shell with her beak, and the crack became the first horizon.

Through the opening drifted a green pebble, pulsing like a sleeping heart. Ivara warmed it beneath her wing until it unfolded into land. Wherever her shadow passed, forests gathered; wherever her tears fell, springs awakened and ran laughing toward the sea.

Still the music sounded, lonely and afraid. Ivara plucked seven downy feathers and laid them in the river mud. At morning they stood as people, wet-eyed and wondering. They asked where to go, so she drew paths of water. They asked what to remember, so she lifted droplets into the night.

The droplets hardened into stars, each holding a note of the deep song. When travelers lose the road, rivers murmur below and stars answer above, guiding them back to the place where the crane first opened the world. And when children dream of wings, their elders say Ivara is turning in sleep, making another dawn inside the dark waters for them all.

Myth: In the elder dark, earth was a closed seed, and silence lay thick upon it. Beneath its shell slept Maro, the Stone Father, with a coal-bright heart. Above him wandered Niva, a star without a road, fallen from the sky’s torn hem.

Each night Niva sang upward. No answer came. Her tears sank through dust and gathered in hidden hollows, until cold fingers touched Maro’s face. He woke, and his yawn split the seed of the world. Valleys opened. Hills rose like shoulders. The hidden tears rushed out as rivers, laughing because they had found motion.

“Little light,” Maro said, “why do you sorrow?”

“My sisters burn beyond reach,” Niva answered.

Maro piled cliffs, but they crumbled. He raised trees, but they bent. At last he broke a glowing shard from his heart and placed it in the dark. It became the moon, a silver path wide enough for one small star.

Niva climbed home. Before leaving, she kissed the rivers and taught them the shape of longing. Since then, waters run onward, never resting, and at night they shine with moonfire, remembering the star who first showed them the way back to heaven.

Myth: Before morning found its golden tongue, the world slept curled inside a stone seed. Around it moved Veyra, a lost star-maiden, trailing dust like torn silk. Beneath the shell rested Aruk, the Mountain Maker, whose heart burned red in the dark.

Veyra called to the heavens, but the heavens were shut. Her song fell as tears and seeped through the seed. They gathered around Aruk’s ears, cold and bright, until he woke and stretched. His shoulders cracked the shell. Out spilled valleys, plains, and black cliffs. The tears escaped, becoming rivers that ran fast because they feared the dark behind them.

“Why do you weep, sky-child?” asked Aruk.

“My sisters shine where I cannot climb,” said Veyra.

Aruk built a ladder of peaks, yet each summit broke beneath the sky. Then he reached into his chest and drew out one ember of his heart. He hung it high, and it cooled into the moon, a pale bridge over night.

Veyra crossed it. Before she vanished, she touched every river with her silver hand. Thus rivers remember the road upward, though they must flow downward, and their moonlit glitter is the sorrow and joy of going home.
